name: Macrophage
blurb: A human macrophage: a large, irregular roaming cell with a ruffled surface and finger-like feet, an oval nucleus with a dent in it, and many lysosomes for digesting what it swallows.
note: Model: a human macrophage, cut through its middle. Measured in humans: its size (diameter and volume, from macrophages washed out of the lungs of healthy non-smokers), the shares of a blood monocyte's volume taken by nucleus, mitochondria and granules, and the descriptions of its oval, dented nucleus, ruffled surface and many lysosomes. Illustrative: the exact outline, the number and length of the feet and ruffles, the nucleus share (a monocyte's share, 26%, shrinks as the cell grows, so 10% is a guess), the number and size of lysosomes and mitochondria, and the colours. Not drawn: the dent in the nucleus, swallowed particles, the endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the cytoskeleton and the receptors on the surface.

diameter.note: mean of human alveolar macrophages from healthy non-smoking volunteers; a macrophage resting in loose connective tissue may differ, and a crawling one is longer than wide; the range (10 to 30) is illustrative, only the mean is measured

volume.note: the same human alveolar macrophages, by flow cytometry; the range is illustrative
volume.compare: the drawn ellipsoid, 24 x 20 x 20 µm, is 5027 µm³

axes.calc: pi/6 x 24 x 20 x 20 = 5027 um3, within 1% of the measured volume
axes.note: illustrative: a cell a little longer than wide, as one on the move is; the axes 24 x 20 x 20 are chosen to give the measured volume

monocyte_nucleus_share.note: nucleus 25.9% of the volume of a human blood monocyte, the cell a macrophage grows from; not a macrophage figure

volume_fraction.calc: a blood monocyte's nucleus is 25.9% of its volume (schmid1980); monocytes grown into macrophages swell three- to four-fold while the nuclear surface grows only a little (sokol1987), so about 26% / 3.5 = 7%, nudged up to 10% because the nucleus does grow some; no study of a human macrophage's nucleus share was opened

nucleus.note: Oval and often dented, a mark of its origin in the monocyte; the dent is not drawn.

volume_fraction.calc: 3.5% of a human blood monocyte's volume (schmid1980); mitochondrial volume rises as monocytes become macrophages (sokol1987), by an amount not found, so the share is a stand-in

count.calc: illustrative: 'numerous' lysosomes (digihisto13); a monocyte's granules, among them its lysosome-like ones, take 2.6% of its volume (schmid1980), which would be several thousand small ones, so far more than are drawn

size_um.note: illustrative; they vary in size and look (digihisto14)

stacks.note: illustrative: one stack, drawn beside the nucleus

not_drawn: swallowed particles and the phagosomes round them

special.note: The surface is heavily folded and ruffled, and the cell puts out broad feet (pseudopodia) to crawl and to wrap round what it swallows (openstax_innate; uribe2020: the feet are built by growth of actin filaments). The fold pattern, five feet and their 7 µm length are illustrative.

A particle larger than 0.5 µm is enclosed in a bag of membrane (a phagosome), which fuses with lysosomes to become a phagolysosome, as acid as pH 4.5 inside (uribe2020; openstax_innate). Only the waiting lysosomes are drawn; swallowed particles are not.
Some macrophages roam the tissue, moving by amoeboid crawling; others are fixed and stay in their tissue for good. The drawn cell is not marked as one or the other.

cut: The cell is cut through its middle: a ruffled outline with a few blunt feet, one oval nucleus with a nucleolus off to one side, mitochondria scattered through the cytoplasm, a stack of Golgi next to the nucleus and many small lysosomes of different sizes among them.

colours.convention: Cell membrane pale pink, the cytoplasm dark; nucleus violet; mitochondria orange; Golgi yellow; lysosomes olive green. All the colours are a code: a living macrophage is almost colourless, and these are the stains and the shading of a picture.

cytosol.name: Cytoplasm
cytosol.about: The watery inside of the cell, crowded with proteins and with the many lysosomes and swallowed particles that fill a macrophage.

about: A macrophage of a person. Its size is that measured for human macrophages washed out of the lungs of healthy non-smokers: 21 µm across and about 4990 µm³ (the drawn cell holds {drawn.cellVolume} µm³). One in loose connective tissue or in the blood-vessel wall may differ in size, and a crawling one is longer than it is wide.

It begins as a monocyte of the blood, leaves a vessel and grows into a macrophage in the tissue. A monocyte's nucleus is about a quarter of the cell; as the cell swells three- to four-fold the nucleus share falls, and 10% is drawn (a guess). The nucleus is oval and, in life, often dented.

Its work is to swallow microbes, dead cells and debris. The surface is folded and ruffled and the cell puts out feet around what it takes in; the swallowed bag then fuses with lysosomes. {drawn.lysosomes} lysosomes are drawn in this half; a real cell has far more, of many sizes, and often particles in the middle of digestion, which are not drawn.

krombach1997.cite: Krombach F, Münzing S, Allmeling AM, Gerlach JT, Behr J, Dörger M (1997) Cell size of alveolar macrophages: an interspecies comparison, Environ Health Perspect 105(Suppl 5):1261-1263
krombach1997.used_for: human alveolar macrophages of healthy non-smokers: diameter 21.2 ± 0.3 µm, volume 4990 ± 174 µm³ (flow cytometry)

schmid1980.cite: Schmid-Schönbein GW, Shih YY, Chien S (1980) Morphometry of human leukocytes, Blood 56(5):866-875, Table 2; read in the BioNumbers entry (BNID 115196), not in the paper
schmid1980.used_for: human blood monocyte, stereology of electron micrographs: nucleus 25.9%, granules 2.6%, mitochondria 3.5%, cytoplasm 68.1% of cell volume

sokol1987.cite: Sokol RJ, Hudson G, James NT, Frost IJ, Wales J (1987) Human macrophage development: a morphometric study, J Anat 151:27-35 (abstract opened only)
sokol1987.used_for: over six days in culture the cell volume rises three- to four-fold, the surface more than doubles with more irregularity, mitochondrial volume rises and the nuclear surface grows only a little (abstract; no absolute values)

openstax_innate.cite: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response
openstax_innate.used_for: a macrophage is an irregularly shaped amoeboid phagocyte that grows from a monocyte, moves by pseudopodia, and engulfs a pathogen into a phagosome that fuses with a lysosome

openstax_ct.cite: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 4.3 Connective Tissue Supports and Protects
openstax_ct.used_for: roaming macrophages move by amoeboid movement; fixed macrophages are permanent residents of their tissues; they come from monocytes

digihisto13.cite: Digital Histology, Connective Tissue Proper, Cells 13 (Macrophage)
digihisto13.used_for: nucleus oval and often indented; cytoplasm with numerous lysosomes and swallowed material; a heavily folded and ruffled surface

digihisto14.cite: Digital Histology, Connective Tissue Proper, Cells 14 (electron micrograph of a macrophage)
digihisto14.used_for: prominent nuclear indentation; heterochromatin along the nuclear envelope; numerous lysosomes of varied appearance; prominent folding and ruffling of the processes

uribe2020.cite: Uribe-Querol E, Rosales C (2020) Phagocytosis: Our Current Understanding of a Universal Biological Process, Front Immunol 11:1066
uribe2020.used_for: phagocytosis is of particles over 0.5 µm; feet are built by actin growth; the phagosome fuses with lysosomes, reaching pH as low as 4.5 (first 100,000 characters read)
